The image is thesis p. 73 (PDF page 104) and carries the passage word for word: "Most Zone F languages have a 7-vowel system with a short-long vowel contrast, but many of the scholars do not show vowel length in their writings nor the 7 vowels. All the languages in the zone are also tonal, but the tones are not always shown partly because of the excuse that it is difficult to mark them and the context can always disambiguate words." The section is a survey of earlier Zone F descriptions (orthography/nomenclature problems), so the sentence is a zone-wide characteri…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress rule is stated for Sumbwa in any opened source. Masele (a Zone F specialist reporting his own transcribed data from three Sumbwa dialects, F23a-c, among 22 varieties) states that every Zone F language, Sumbwa included, is tonal with contrastive vowel length; he never mentions stress or accent. Capus 1898 (the only full grammar) is likewise silent on accent. The only prosodic-prominence remark is Masele p. 178: a tentative SSN (Sumbwa-Sukuma-Nyamwezi) tendency for penultimate syllables of some verbs to lengthen their vowels, which he treats as vowel length conditioned phonologically/semantically/phonetically and immediately qualifies with counterexamples.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: For the penultimate-lengthening tendency (p. 178): 'penultimate position may be true in some dialects, although not only that in JinaKiiya, because -fuulila "blow in order to soothe" and -pulila "snatch for (someone)" violate that rule' (examples are Sukuma, not Sumbwa).
new_statements.domain_note: The tonal statement is zone-level (all Guthrie Zone F languages), applied to SiSuumbwa by inclusion; Masele's data were elicited words in isolation from a 28-page questionnaire with surface tones marked. The p. 178 lengthening remark concerns verb stems in SSN generally.
new_statements.identity_note: Capus 1898 describes 'Shisumbwa ou Lusumbwa' of Ushirombo (the same F23, sumb1240), noting Kifyoma as identical. Masele 2001 treats SiSuumbwa (F23) as three dialects: SiSiloombo (F23a), SiYoombe (F23b), KiLoongo (F23c); his tonal statement covers all Zone F languages, so it applies to Sumbwa only by inclusion, not as a Sumbwa-specific analysis.

sources.note: No word-stress/accent statement anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent|accent|penult over the full text). p. 73: all Zone F languages (incl. SiSuumbwa F23 with dialects SiSiloombo F23a, SiYoombe F23b, KiLoongo F23c) are tonal with a short-long vowel contrast, tones often left unmarked by earlier writers. p. 178: 'it might be a rule in SSN which states that penultimate syllables tend to lengthen their vowels in some verbs' — a vowel-length tendency illustrated from JinaKiiya (Sukuma), with counterexamples; not framed as stress.

Only Nurse 2000 (classification) and Eberhard et al. 2025 visible in the rendered page; the local our source list record already lists the 6 descriptive refs (Kahigi 1977 x2, 1988, 2000, 2005; Capus 1898).

sources.citation: Capus, Auguste. 1898. Grammaire de Shisumbwa. Zeitschrift für afrikanische und oceanische Sprachen 4: 1-123. Berlin: Reimer.
sources.note: Silent. 'Notions préliminaires' (pp. 2-3) is a letter-by-letter pronunciation key plus a remark that vowels are short or long and distinguish meanings; the only 'accentué' is a remark that some loanwords have a more strongly articulated k (p. 3); the only 'ton' (p. 89) is sentence intonation disambiguating scornful/admiring readings of augmentative/diminutive prefixes. Whole grammar (BSB scanned, scan pp. 7-129) searched for accent/tonique/intonation/ton/syllabe/prosod: no word-stress or accent statement.
Nothing on phonology; states the language 'is still largely undescribed' apart from Capus 1898, Kahigi 2005/2008a/2008b and Masele 2001.
